subtopic: Deciding whether to join a protest
subtype: Approach: joining because friends are going [Pitfall]
passage: I'm Anirban, and I was standing two rows behind Abhinav at the rally. On Friday he had said, “Everyone from tuition is going, so I'm going,” and when I asked what the march wanted, he shrugged and laughed. Today he waved a paper flag at strangers. Then the crowd near the barricade began shoving, and somebody shouted that the road was closing. Abhinav's laugh stopped. “Which way is the gate?” he asked me. I didn't know either; neither of us had checked. He grabbed his friend's sleeve and we pushed sideways for ten minutes, his water bottle gone and his phone nearly dead. I can't say what he felt, but he kept muttering, “What are we even here for?” Finally a shopkeeper let us sit inside, and Abhinav rang his mother from the shop.

qa.q: Why did Abhinav go to the rally?
qa.a: Everyone from tuition was going, so he went too.

qa.q: What might Abhinav have been feeling when he asked which way the gate was?
qa.a: Fear and confusion: his laugh stopped and he kept asking what they were there for, which suggests he did not know what he was supporting or how to leave.

qa.q: What could Abhinav have done before going, and why would it help?
qa.a: He could have found out what the march demanded and agreed a leaving route and a check-in with a parent, because then he would know what he was backing and how to get out.

qa.q: How does the day look to Anirban, who tagged along?
qa.a: Anirban was pulled into the same confusion with no exit plan either, and could only guess at Abhinav's feelings while trying to find a safe way out.

grounding: A teen joins a protest because friends do, without knowing the demands, and is lost when tension rises.
